units.name: Democracy
units.summary: What democracy requires beyond simply holding a vote.

topics.name: What Democracy Requires
topics.summary: Voting is necessary but not sufficient.

objectives.text: Say why elections alone are not sufficient.
Describe what protects a minority from a majority.

keyTerms.definition: A system where political power comes from the people.
Those in power having to answer for what they do.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body:
Democracy is often summarised as "the people vote". Voting is necessary, but a vote on its own does not make a system democratic. This lesson is about what else is required.

Scope note: this teaches the general principles, which are shared across democracies. It does not describe Liberia’s specific electoral arrangements — for those, use the Constitution or your teacher’s materials.

sections.heading: The basic idea
sections.body:
In a DEMOCRACY, political power comes from the people. Those who govern do so because the people chose them, and they can be removed the same way.

The contrast is with a system where rulers hold power by force, by inheritance, or by their own say-so, and the governed have no means of changing them.

sections.heading: Why voting is not enough
sections.body:
Imagine a country that holds an election, but:

    newspapers may not criticise the government
    opposition candidates are arrested
    voters are told who to choose and watched while voting
    the people counting the votes work for one candidate

An election happened. Was it democratic?

No. A vote only expresses the people's will if people can find out what is going on, choose freely, and have their choice counted honestly.

So democracy also requires:

    FREE EXPRESSION — you can criticise those in power without punishment
    REAL CHOICE — genuine alternatives are allowed to stand
    A SECRET BALLOT — nobody can punish you for how you voted
    AN HONEST COUNT — results reflect the votes cast
    ACCOUNTABILITY — those in power must answer for what they do
    RULE OF LAW — leaders are subject to the law like everyone else

Remove any one and the election becomes a ceremony rather than a decision.

sections.heading: The majority does not get everything
sections.body:
Democracy means the majority decides — but not that the majority may do anything at all.

If 60% could vote to remove the rights of the other 40%, then those 40% have no rights, only permissions that can be withdrawn. And a majority is not fixed: today's majority can be tomorrow's minority.

This is why constitutions put certain things beyond an ordinary vote, and why courts can strike down a law even when it was passed by a majority. Those limits are not undemocratic. They are what stops democracy consuming itself.
sections.example:
Two decisions, one town.

A town votes on where to build a new well. The majority chooses the east side. That is democracy working — a shared decision, made by the most people, and next year they could choose differently.

Now the town votes that families from one clan may not use the well at all.

The same procedure was followed. The majority still won. But this decision removes a basic entitlement from a group because they are outnumbered — and no vote count makes that legitimate.

The difference is not how the decision was made. It is what the decision does.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. Give two conditions besides voting that democracy requires, and explain what each protects.
2. Why is a secret ballot important? What could happen without it?
3. Explain why "the majority voted for it" does not always make something acceptable.
4. Using your Constitution or class materials, find how elections are arranged in Liberia, and note anything that differs from the general picture here.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• Democracy means power comes from the people and rulers can be replaced.
• Voting alone is not enough: free expression, real choice, a secret ballot, an honest count, accountability and rule of law are all required.
• Majorities decide, but may not remove others’ basic rights.
• Limits on the majority protect democracy rather than weaken it.

questions.question: A country holds elections, but newspapers may not criticise the government and opposition candidates are arrested. Is this democratic?
options: No — voting alone is not enough without free expression and real choice
Only if the count was accurate
questions.explanation: A vote expresses the people’s will only if they can find out what is happening, choose freely, and have the choice counted honestly. Without free expression and genuine alternatives, the election is a ceremony rather than a decision.

questions.question: Why do democracies limit what a majority may vote to do?
options: Because a majority removing others’ basic rights would leave those people with no rights at all
They do not — a majority may decide anything
questions.explanation: If 60% could vote away the rights of the other 40%, those 40% would hold only permissions that could be withdrawn. A majority is not fixed either — today’s majority may be tomorrow’s minority. Such limits protect democracy rather than weaken it.
